newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Asian traders wary on Cargill barter with N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: Asian traders wary on Cargill barter with N.Korea.

text.p: Asian traders with North Korea experience on Tuesday said they were sceptical about plans by U.S. grains giant Cargill Inc to barter as much as two million tonnes of grain with Pyongyang.
"According to our experience, trade with North Korea will face great difficulty, such as honouring agreements and making payments," said an official at a South Korean trading house.
On Monday, Cargill said it was awaiting a decision by the U.S. Treasury Department on an application to barter grain for North Korean commodities.
An initial 500,000 tonne grain shipment was envisaged.
Cargill said the application, submitted in September, simply sought authorisation for barter dealing of some food product but did not specify whether rice, corn or other commodities would be traded.
Minneapolis-based Cargill is the world's largest private grain-trading company.
U.S. officials said they were considering easing trade sanctions against North Korea -- which is reeling from flood-induced food shortages -- to allow barter deals.
On Sunday, North Korea apologised for the first time for an incursion by one of its submarines into South Korean waters in September, expressing "deep regret" in a brief statement.

The statement was issued after intense bargaining in New York between U.S. and North Korean officials on a choice of words to make the apology acceptable to Seoul, which branded the incursion a "military provocation".
One Hong Kong-based grains trader said securing payment from North Korea for barter trade would not be easy.
"Banks in North Korea are not reliable and letters of credit can be worthless," he said.
"The logistics are terrible and the risk is enormous," he said, noting that the quality of goods received from North Korea in a barter exchange was difficult to control.
In one instance, a barter deal previously arranged by the trader fell through, resulting in losses.
"They got the cargo of wheat, we never got the cargo of metals and the guy just disappeared," he said.
South Korean traders said they doubted Cargill could handle a deal the size of two million tonnes of grain, the maximum asked for in its application.
"The key to Cargill's food aid is how Cargill is to be paid," a senior trader in a Seoul-based foreign grains-trading company said.
"The amount of food barter by Cargill will vary according to the North's ability to pay," a South Korean Foreign Ministry official said.

North Korea had limited goods to offer, but was rich in coal and anthracite, the Hong Kong trader noted. It also had goods such as VAM monomers and polypropelene -- the building blocks of complex industrial chemicals.
A South Korean metals trader said the North may ship lead and zinc in exchange for food while a Seoul Foreign Ministry official said magnesites could be offered.
"North Korea apologised because they are desperate (for food)," the Hong Kong trader said.
